sentences.text: Here's one question, written two ways: as DataFrame code, and as SQL. Higher-risk patients, counted by clinic.
Which one runs faster? Neither. Spark turns both into the same plan, step for step.
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: say what, not how.
First, Spark reads what you wrote and looks up every name: the table, and each column, with its type.
In classic PySpark, that happens line by line, as you write.
So a misspelt column fails right there, on its own line, before a single task runs.
Over Spark Connect, DataFrame code waits until its plan is first needed, but a SQL string still fails at once.
Then the optimiser rewrites the plan. It adds a check you never wrote: that x isn't null. And it keeps only what the query needs: clinic, for the count.
It reorders what's safe to reorder, too. Write a filter on clinic after the count, and the optimiser moves it before: fewer rows to count.
You said what you wanted. Spark chose the steps.

Last, Spark picks real operators. It hands the read a copy of the filter, so the read can skip what can't match, and has it read only 2 of the 4 columns. The filter still runs after the read, to be sure.
And the one count becomes two: a partial count on each pile, an exchange, and a final count. That's Episode 4's wall.

Explain, formatted, shows the physical plan, node by node: the scan, with the filters it was handed and the two columns it reads; then the filter, the partial count, the exchange, and the final count.
Before a run, it's the starting plan: adaptive execution can still change it. That's episode 12.
Here's why handing the filter down pays. Take the cast ten thousand times over, sorted by risk, in one file of 25 row groups.
Each group records the smallest and largest x it holds.

With the filter handed down, the reader skips the 13 groups that can't hold a higher-risk patient. Of the 12 it reads, it needs just two columns: about 2.6 kilobytes of column data, where all four would be nearly 2 megabytes.
Those sizes belong to this sorted file. Unsorted, every group holds both kinds, and nothing is skipped.
Turn pushdown off, and every group is read.
Now write the same filter as a Python function. To Spark, it's a black box.
It can't hand the filter to the read, so every row is read, and for every row the value it checks, x, travels to Python and back, just to be checked.
On our sorted file, that's all 25 row groups instead of 12. Keep your logic where the optimiser can see it.
Let's gather it up.
Say what you want, in DataFrame code or in SQL: it's the same plan. Spark checks the names, rewrites the plan, reads only what it needs, and picks the operators.
A Python function hides its logic, and the optimiser can't help.
The plan is chosen. But is it cheap? Next time, Part Two begins: counting walls.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
